content.text: Oscillatory motion is repetitive to-and-fro motion about a mean or equilibrium position. Examples include a swinging pendulum, a boat moving up and down, a piston moving back and forth, vibrating strings and membranes, and atoms vibrating about equilibrium positions. Periodic motion repeats after a fixed interval; not all periodic motion is oscillatory.
A motion is periodic if its state repeats after a fixed time interval. The least positive time after which the motion repeats is its period T. Motion may be periodic without being simple harmonic.

In oscillatory motion, a body moves to and fro around a mean position. At stable equilibrium the net force is zero; when displaced slightly, a restoring force can tend to return the body toward equilibrium.

The time period T is the time for one complete oscillation. Frequency ν is the number of oscillations per unit time. They are reciprocals: T = 1/ν and ν = 1/T. The SI unit of frequency is hertz (Hz), equal to one cycle per second.
Displacement x is measured from the equilibrium position. Amplitude A is the maximum magnitude of displacement. In ideal SHM, amplitude is constant when damping is absent.
For x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ), the phase is ωt + φ and the phase constant φ specifies the initial state of oscillation. Phase distinguishes where in the cycle the oscillator is at a given time.
Angular frequency ω measures phase change per unit time and is related to period and frequency by ω = 2π/T = 2πν. Its SI unit is rad s⁻¹.

Simple harmonic motion (SHM) is oscillatory motion in which acceleration is directly proportional to displacement from equilibrium and directed oppositely: a = −ω²x. Equivalently, the restoring force is F = −kx for a mass m, with ω² = k/m.
A standard displacement expression for SHM is x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ). Equivalent sine/cosine forms can represent the same motion when amplitude and phase are chosen consistently.

SHM can be represented as the projection of uniform circular motion onto a diameter. If a point moves uniformly on a circle of radius A, its projection has displacement x = A cos(ωt + φ) and executes SHM.

content.text: Differentiating x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ) gives v(t) = −ωA sin(ωt + φ). The maximum speed is v_max = ωA. Speed is zero at the extreme positions and greatest at equilibrium.
The acceleration is a(t) = −ω²A cos(ωt + φ) = −ω²x(t), so its maximum magnitude is a_max = ω²A. Acceleration is zero at equilibrium and has greatest magnitude at the extremes.

Displacement, velocity and acceleration vary sinusoidally with the same period but differ in phase. Velocity is shifted by a quarter cycle relative to displacement; acceleration is opposite in sign to displacement.
For a mass m in SHM, F = ma = −mω²x. Comparing with Hooke’s law F = −kx gives k = mω² and ω = √(k/m). The restoring force always points toward equilibrium.
For a mass m attached to an ideal spring of force constant k, ω = √(k/m) and T = 2π√(m/k). In the ideal linear model, the period is independent of amplitude.
The kinetic energy is K = ½mv². Using v² = ω²(A² − x²), K = ½mω²(A² − x²) = ½k(A² − x²) for a spring oscillator.
For an ideal spring oscillator, the potential energy relative to equilibrium is U = ½kx² = ½mω²x². It is minimum at equilibrium and maximum at the turning points.
Without friction or other energy loss, total mechanical energy remains constant: E = K + U = ½kA² = ½mω²A². Kinetic and potential energies continually transform into each other.
At equilibrium x = 0, potential energy is zero relative to equilibrium and kinetic energy is maximum. At x = ±A, velocity and kinetic energy are zero while potential energy is maximum.
A simple pendulum consists of a small bob suspended by a light, inextensible string of length L from a fixed support. For small angular displacement, the restoring torque leads approximately to SHM.
For small oscillations, the angular equation is approximately θ¨ = −(g/L)θ. Thus ω = √(g/L) and the period is T = 2π√(L/g).

The simple-pendulum period formula assumes small angular oscillations and negligible damping, with a fixed support and uniform gravitational field. The period depends on length and g, and in this approximation does not depend on bob mass or amplitude.
For small θ measured in radians, sin θ ≈ θ. This converts the pendulum restoring torque equation into a linear equation and makes the motion approximately simple harmonic.
For a given angular frequency, two independent initial conditions determine the motion, such as initial position and velocity, or amplitude and phase. The phase constant encodes the initial state.
The forms x = A cos(ωt + φ), x = A cos ωt + B sin ωt, and corresponding sine forms are equivalent representations when their constants are related appropriately.

Every SHM is periodic in the ideal undamped case, but every periodic motion is not SHM. SHM specifically requires a linear restoring force, F = −kx, or acceleration proportional and opposite to displacement.

Real oscillators can lose mechanical energy through friction or resistance, causing amplitude to decrease. Damped motion is not strictly SHM, although it may approximate SHM over short time intervals when damping is weak.
A sum of two SHMs with arbitrary frequencies and phases is not always periodic. The combined motion is periodic when the frequency ratio is rational; otherwise it generally does not repeat exactly.

A particle subject to a restoring force proportional to its position vector can move in a circle for suitable initial conditions. Equal angular frequencies in perpendicular directions with a quarter-cycle phase difference produce circular motion.
For an oscillator with amplitude A and angular frequency ω, maximum speed is v_max = ωA. If the stroke of a piston is specified as twice the amplitude, then A equals half the stroke.
The maximum acceleration magnitude in SHM is a_max = ω²A. Acceleration points toward equilibrium and is largest at the endpoints.
For a spring-mass system, the angular frequency follows from the restoring force and Newton’s second law: ω = √(k/m). Increasing mass lengthens the period; increasing spring stiffness shortens it.
For the same pendulum length, the period scales as 1/√g. Therefore the period on a body with smaller gravitational acceleration is longer by the factor √(g_earth/g_body).

content.text: Periodic motion repeats after a period T; frequency ν = 1/T. SHM displacement is x = A cos(ωt + φ), with ω = 2π/T = 2πν. Velocity v = −ωA sin(ωt + φ), acceleration a = −ω²x, and restoring force F = −kx.
For an ideal SHM oscillator, K = ½mv², U = ½kx², and E = K + U = ½kA² remains constant. For a spring-mass system T = 2π√(m/k); for a simple pendulum at small angles T = 2π√(L/g).
The period is the least positive time after which motion repeats. The motion repeats after integer multiples nT, where n is an integer.
For ideal linear SHM, the period is independent of amplitude, energy and phase constant. This is a property of the linear restoring-force model.
A simple pendulum executes approximately SHM only for small angular displacement. At larger amplitudes, the small-angle approximation is no longer accurate.

content.text: Which of the following examples represent periodic motion? (a) A swimmer completing one (return) trip from one bank of a river to the other and back. (b) A freely suspended bar magnet displaced from its N-S direction and released. (c) A hydrogen molecule rotating about its centre of mass. (d) An arrow released from a bow.

(d) general vibrations of a polyatomic molecule about its equilibrium position.
